bio: Khawar Shahzad hosts Muffled Minds. This first Muffled Minds documentary is narrated in Urdu over animations of the Earth and the Sun; no guest appears in the episode and the narration does not introduce a host on camera.

In this documentary the narration explains how the rotation of the Earth makes day and night, why the 23.5 degree tilt of the Earth makes the seasons, and why the Arctic and Antarctic get six months of daylight and then six months of darkness.

summary: The Earth looks completely peaceful from above, but it never stops, not even for a moment. This first Muffled Minds documentary explains, in Urdu, how the Earth spins silently on its axis, and how that spinning holds the whole story of day and night: when a part of the Earth faces the Sun, day breaks out there, and as that part turns away, the light fades into evening and then night. The Sun does not go anywhere and does not hide; the Earth turns, and the light changes with it.

Then the documentary turns to the seasons. Summer and winter do not come from the heat of the Sun, but from the 23.5 degree tilt of the Earth. As the Earth makes its huge circle around the Sun through the year, different parts receive light from different angles: direct light brings long days and summer, slanted light brings short days and winter, which is why one part of the world can have summer while another part has winter at the same time.

The last part covers the most astonishing phenomenon of all: at the Arctic and the Antarctic, day lasts for six months and night for six months. When the tilted Earth keeps its upper part facing the Sun, the Sun does not set at all, shining 24 hours a day for months, the midnight sun. Six months later that same polar region has turned away from the Sun and darkness covers it for six months, the polar night. It closes with the thought that day and night, the seasons, months-long polar nights and never-ending days are all part of the beautiful, never-ending journey of the Earth.

takeaways: The Sun does not rise or set: the Earth spins on its axis, and the part facing the Sun has day.
Day, afternoon and evening are all the same motion: the Earth turning on its axis.
It is not the heat of the Sun that makes the seasons, but the 23.5 degree tilt of the Earth.
When a part of the Earth is close to the Sun and in direct light, it has summer; when it moves away, the light falls slanted and winter begins.
That is why one part of the world can have summer while another part has winter at the same time.
At the poles the Sun does not set for six months, the midnight sun, and then darkness lasts six months, the polar night.

Jab koi hissa sooraj ke kareeb aur seedhi roshni mein hota hai, to wahan garmi aati hai. Log dhoop mein chalte nazar aate hain, din lambe hote hain, sooraj upar dikhai deta hai. Aur jab wahi hissa sooraj se door ho jaata hai, roshni tirchhi padti hai, din chhote ho jaate hain aur sardi shuru ho jaati hai. Yahi wajah hai ke duniya ke ek hisse mein garmi aur doosre hisse mein usi waqt sardi hoti hai. Aur ab sab se hairaan-kun hissa: zameen ke kuch aise ilaake bhi hain, khaas taur par qutub shumali yaani Arctic aur qutub junoobi Antarctica, jahan chhe maheene tak din rehta hai aur chhe maheene tak raat.

Yeh kyun hota hai? Kyunki jab zameen jhuk kar sooraj ke gird ghoomti hai, to kabhi aisa waqt aata hai ke zameen ka poora upar wala hissa sooraj ki taraf jhuka rehta hai. Isi dauraan wahan sooraj doobta hi nahin. Log dekhte hain ke raat hone ke waqt bhi sooraj aasmaan mein maujood rehta hai, jise midnight sun kaha jaata hai. 24 ghante sooraj, aur yeh silsila kai maheenon tak chalta rehta hai. Phir 6 maah baad zameen apni gardish mein aise muqaam par pahunchti hai ke wahi qutubi hissa sooraj se door chala jaata hai. Tab wahan chhe maheene ki tareeki chha jaati hai. Sooraj aasmaan par nazar hi nahin aata. Din ho ya raat, har waqt ek jaisa andhera. Is tareeki ko polar night kehte hain.

Yaani zameen ke jhukaav aur iske saalana safar ki wajah se duniya ke kuch hisse maheenon tak roshni mein nahaate rehte hain, aur kuch maheenon tak mukammal andhere mein rehte hain. Din raat ka badlna, mausamon ka aana-jaana, qutbon par maheenon lambi raatein aur na khatm hone wale din — yeh sab zameen ki khoobsurat harkaton ka hissa hai. transcript_en.text: This world looks completely peaceful from above, but in reality it does not stop even for a moment. Our Earth keeps spinning silently on its axis, and in this spinning lies the whole story of day and night. When a part of the Earth faces the Sun, day breaks out there, and as soon as that part moves away from the Sun, the light fades, evening falls, and then complete night spreads. Neither does the Sun go anywhere, nor does it hide anywhere — the Earth just keeps spinning, and the light keeps changing with it. We think the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, but the reality is that we ourselves are moving past the Sun. Day, afternoon, evening — all of it is the play of the Earth's movement. But now, let's come to the seasons: the real secret of summer and winter is

not the Sun's heat, but the Earth's tilt of 23.5 degrees. The Earth makes one huge circle around the Sun all year, and during this, different parts receive light from different angles. When a part is close to the Sun and in direct light, summer comes there. People are seen walking in the sunlight, days are long, the Sun appears high above. And when that same part moves away from the Sun, the light falls slanted, days get shorter and winter begins. That is why one part of the world has summer while another part has winter at the same time. And now the most astonishing part: there are some regions of the Earth, especially the North Pole, the Arctic, and the South Pole, Antarctica, where day lasts for six months and night for six months.

Why does this happen? Because when the Earth orbits the Sun on its tilt, there comes a time when the entire upper part of the Earth stays tilted towards the Sun. During this time, the Sun does not set there at all. People see that even at night time, the Sun is still in the sky — this is called the midnight sun. 24 hours of Sun, and this goes on for many months. Then, 6 months later, the Earth reaches a point in its orbit where that same polar region moves away from the Sun. Then six months of darkness fall there. The Sun is not seen in the sky at all. Whether it is day or night, there is the same darkness all the time. This darkness is called the polar night.

So, because of the Earth's tilt and its yearly journey, some parts of the world bathe in light for months, and some stay in complete darkness for months. The changing of day and night, the coming and going of seasons, months-long nights at the poles and never-ending days — all of this is part of the Earth's beautiful movements. So next time you see the Sun rise, see the stars at night, or feel summer and winter, remember: all of this is because of that great, constant journey of our Earth.
